prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

More than a hundred dollars of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass things to stuff them in. Now a white and purple cloud is breathing in each corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table— each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I watch children shuffle strictly in line, cradle candles that dribbled hot white on their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad? Didn't I use to go mucking through streambeds with the skunk cabbage raising bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies and smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights have to be not switched on. And in close darkness the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does. I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring and one tall room and the tremble of my phone. I'm not the only one that love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being ripped to prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun I feel I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: More, Now, Didn

outputs.L1: More than a hundred dollars' worth of them. It was pure folly. I had to scour the house for more glass vessels to hold them all. Now a white and purple cloud breathes in every corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table—each blossom fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I once watch children shuffle in strict procession, cradling candles that dribbled hot wax across their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad then? Didn't I used to go wading through streambeds where skunk cabbage thrust up its bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon is dying as night gathers in the heart of the lilies, smoking up their fluted throats until it fills the room, and I cannot bring myself to switch on the lights. In that close darkness the fragrance swells so sweet, so potent, that it could cut me open. It does. I know I am not the only one whose life hangs like a conditional clause from something to do with spring, one tall room, and the tremble of a phone. I am not the only one whom love unravels like a dozen flapping bedsheets torn into prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sunlight, I feel as though I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.
outputs.L2:
I spent well over a hundred dollars on them—an utterly reckless purchase. Afterward, I scrambled to find enough vases and jars to contain them all. Now, in every corner of this room I cherish, clusters of white and purple blooms seem to pulse like breathing clouds. My dining table, too, disappears beneath an overflow of blossoms, each one youthful and vibrant, unfurling tender leaves into the tangled abundance.

Do I still remember watching children move in solemn procession, holding candles that let hot wax drip onto their small hands as they recited Latin prayers, building Seville's Holy Week traditions? Was there sorrow in me then? Do I recall wading through creek beds, marveling at skunk cabbage thrusting up its violet-tinged shoots?

Watch now: daylight fades as evening settles into the core of these lilies, releasing its haze until it drifts through their trumpet-shaped petals and saturates the entire room, leaving me unwilling to flip on any switch. In that gathering dusk, the fragrance intensifies—so rich, so overwhelming, it feels capable of cutting straight through me. And it does.

Surely I'm not alone in living a life suspended, like an unfinished sentence, from something tied to springtime, a single lofty room, and the buzz of an incoming call on my phone. Surely others, too, have felt love unravel them the way wind shreds a row of hanging sheets into fluttering prayer flags. Standing beneath direct sunlight, I sense that I've been tumbling forward, head over heels, for years uncounted. Heavens, how see-through I've become. How weightless.
outputs.L3:
I bought over a hundred dollars' worth of flowers today, which I can only call pure folly. There was no occasion, no anniversary, no apology to make—only a sudden, unreasoning need that seized me in the shop and would not let go until my arms were full of stems. Afterward I had to ransack the house for containers, pressing into service every jar and vase and even a few juice glasses that had no business holding anything so extravagant.

Now the room is transformed. White and purple blooms crowd every corner, spilling from their makeshift vessels and sprawling across the dining table in a tangle of fresh, delicate leaves pressed too close together, as if the flowers themselves were arguing over space. The whole room smells like a decision I can't take back.

I sit among them and old memories surface unbidden. I think of Sevilla, of children in a solemn Easter procession, their faces grave beyond their years, candles dripping wax onto small, careful hands as they walked in a silence that seemed older than the city itself. And I think of another kind of pilgrimage—wading through cold streambeds in early spring, watching skunk cabbage force its strange, hooded shoots up through mud and old snow, proof that even the ugliest things insist on being born.

As the light fails and the room goes dark, the lilies begin to assert themselves. Their scent thickens, grows heavy and sweet, until it seems less like a fragrance than a presence—something that could open me like a blade if I let it. I sit very still in the dark, breathing it in, and feel something in my chest give way.

It occurs to me, in that overwhelmed hour, that my whole life has come to resemble a fragile conditional clause—an *if* that has never quite arrived at its *then*, a sentence that depends entirely on something I cannot name to complete it. I think of love this way too: contingent, unfinished, always bracing for the wind that might tear it apart. And I think of myself as bedsheets torn into prayer flags, thin cotton flapping and fraying in the open air, offering up whatever prayers the wind cares to carry off.

By the time the room is fully dark, I feel strange and light, almost transparent—as though the flowers, the memories, the ache of it all, had passed clean through me and left something thinner and more honest in their place.
outputs.L4:
I did not need them. That is the first thing to understand—I did not need a single stem of what I carried home, arms full, having spent more than a hundred dollars on flowers in the space of twenty impulsive minutes, the way one might spend that same sum on something practical, something defensible. But there was no defending this. There was only the woman at the register asking if I wanted the roses wrapped separately from the ranunculus, and me saying yes, yes, everything separate, everything considered, as if precision in the wrapping could excuse the excess of the buying.

I brought them into the room I love best, the one with the low afternoon light and the window that doesn't quite close, and I began to arrange them without any real plan. The ranunculus first, their tissue-paper petals impossibly layered, then the roses, deep and blowsy, already beginning to open past their prime, and the sprigs of something green and unnamed that the woman had tucked in for free. I filled three vases, then a fourth, a water glass pressed into service because I had run out of proper vessels. I placed them on the windowsill, on the desk, on the floor beside the bed, until the room began to smell like something out of my childhood—thick, floral, almost unbearably sweet.

And it took me back, the way scent does, sideways and without permission, to Sevilla, to standing on my mother's shoulders or perhaps just close against her side, small enough that the world was mostly legs and shadows, watching the Easter procession pass with its towering floats of lilies and carnations, the nazarenos in their peaked hoods moving slow as a held breath, the whole street thick with wax and flowers and a grief so ceremonial it became a kind of festival. I did not understand it then. I only understood the smell, how it filled the space between buildings like water filling a glass, how it made my chest feel strange, too full, as though something in me had been asked to hold more than it was built for.

It took me, too, to the springs of walking through streambeds gone dry or nearly dry, the banks crowded with wildflowers no one had planted, flowers that existed simply because the season demanded them, because the earth could not help itself. I remembered the particular ache of those walks—not sadness, exactly, but a kind of exposure, as if spring stripped something from you, some winter armor, and left you tender to the world in a way you hadn't asked for and couldn't refuse.

Now, in this darkening room, with the scent of a hundred dollars' worth of impulse pressing against the walls, I understood that ache again. The light was going gold and then gray, the way it does in early evening, and the flowers seemed to glow faintly against the dimness, holding onto color the room itself was giving up. I sat on the edge of the bed and let the smell move through me and thought: this is what love does. This is what spring does. They render you helpless in the same instant they render you weightless, as if the self could be both crushed and set free by the same overwhelming thing.

I thought I was alone in this—in the strange, specific vulnerability of loving something so much it becomes indistinguishable from grief, of standing in a room thick with flowers you didn't need and feeling your own edges go soft, your own substance go thin, until you are something closer to light than to matter. I thought this transparency, this fragile and devastating openness, was mine alone to carry.

But it isn't. It never was. It is only the oldest inheritance there is—this susceptibility to beauty, this willingness to be undone by it. Every person who has ever stood in a doorway smelling of lilies, every child lifted up to watch a procession of grief dressed as celebration, every walker along a dry streambed suddenly ambushed by color—all of them have known this same thinning of the self, this same fragile and weightless devastation. Love and spring do not spare us because we are unprepared. They visit everyone equally, indiscriminately, and leave us all a little more transparent than we were, a little more like the flowers themselves: briefly, achingly alive, and already beginning, however slowly, to let go.
outputs.L5:
# More, Now, Didn't

We live in an age obsessed with **more**. More success, more possessions, more experiences to document and share. The message arrives through every screen, every advertisement, every subtle comparison we make with others' curated lives: what you have is not enough. There is always another rung to climb, another milestone to reach, another version of yourself waiting just beyond the horizon of your current achievements.

But somewhere in this endless pursuit, we forget about **now**. The present moment—the only one we actually possess—gets sacrificed on the altar of future gain. We eat dinner while planning tomorrow's meetings. We watch our children play while scrolling through work emails. We stand in beautiful places, cameras raised, already thinking about how the photo will look rather than how the moment feels. The irony is sharp: in chasing more, we lose the very thing that makes any of it meaningful—our attention to what is actually happening in front of us.

And then there's **didn't**. The word that haunts quiet moments, that surfaces in the space between sleep and waking. *I didn't call.* *I didn't say what I meant.* *I didn't take the chance when it was there.* Regret has a particular weight, different from disappointment about things that failed—it's the heaviness of paths never taken, words left unsaid, love not expressed while there was still time.

Perhaps the real wisdom lies in seeing how these three words relate to each other. Our hunger for more often blinds us to now, and it's precisely this blindness that later produces our didn'ts. The person consumed by tomorrow's goals rarely notices today's small opportunities for connection, honesty, or courage—and years later, wonders why so much remains undone, unsaid, unlived.

Maybe the answer isn't to stop wanting more, but to redirect that wanting: more presence, more courage in this moment, more willingness to act now rather than deferring to some imagined future when conditions will finally be right. Because that future has a way of arriving only as another now, equally imperfect, equally demanding of our attention.

The didn'ts of tomorrow are being written in the nows we're neglecting today.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about buying too many flowers on impulse and filling a room with their scent and beauty.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Buying Too Many Flowers

I did not need them—the peonies blushing like a secret told too loudly, the ranunculus curled tight as fists full of small change, the eucalyptus trailing its silver-green hush through everything else. I did not need any of it, and so of course I bought all of it, arms aching with paper cones and stems, the register ringing up my particular madness in a language only the heart speaks fluently: *more, more, this too, and this.*

Now the apartment has become something else entirely. A chapel. A greenhouse. A room that forgot it was a room.

The scent arrives before I do, meets me at the door each time like an animal who has missed me terribly—sweet peas insisting, garden roses murmuring their old velvet rumors, something citrus-bright cutting through the heavier perfumes like a held note. I walk from room to room just to be ambushed again and again by beauty I did not budget for, did not plan, could not justify to anyone who asked *why so many, why all at once, what are you celebrating.*

Nothing. Everything. The Tuesday-ness of Tuesday. The fact that I am alive in a body that can still be stopped mid-step by color.

The vases multiply—water glasses, a chipped teapot, an old jam jar pressed into unlikely service—each one a small rescue, a temporary shelter for these bright and dying things. Because that's the secret truth beneath all this excess: they are already leaving even as they arrive. Every petal is a countdown. Every bloom a held breath about to release.

Maybe that's why I couldn't stop. Maybe abundance is my way of arguing with impermanence—if one stem must wilt, let there be fifty more to distract me from the wilting. Let the whole room hum and blush and drop its confetti of spent petals onto the table, the floor, the pages of the book I meant to read but keep abandoning for this instead: this looking, this breathing in, this quiet astonishment that costs too much and is worth every cent.

Tomorrow the water will need changing. Some blooms will have already given up their brief argument with gravity.

But tonight the whole apartment leans toward yes. Tonight I live inside a held bouquet, extravagant and doomed and gorgeous, and I would not trade this fleeting, ridiculous abundance for anything sensible at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse piece that blends memories of a childhood Easter procession in Sevilla with the overwhelming presence of lilies in a room at dusk.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Lilies

There is a smell that undoes me still—
that thick sweetness lilies carry into a darkening room,
pollen dust settling like the incense
that used to hang above Sevilla's streets
when I was small enough to be lifted
onto my father's shoulders to see the Virgin pass.

Semana Santa. The nazarenos
in their peaked hoods, candles dripping wax
onto cobblestones worn smooth by centuries
of grief and gold. The saeta rising
from some window, raw-throated,
a woman's voice cracking open the night
like a pomegranate spilling its seeds.

I remember the weight of my father's hands
steadying my ankles, the brass band's dirge
moving through my chest before my ears
even understood sorrow as music.
The Virgin's face, tear-streaked in silver,
swaying above the crowd like something
that had learned to walk on human shoulders alone.

Now, in this room, the lilies open
their white throats in the last light,
and I am seven again, held above
a river of black robes and burning wax,
watching my mother cross herself
three times before the float disappeared
around the corner of Calle Sierpes.

The scent is the same devotion—
that same excess, that same insistence
that beauty and grief share a single stem,
that we cannot have the flower
without also having its dying,
the way we cannot have the procession
without the ache that makes us watch it.

Dusk deepens. The lilies do not close.
They hold their whiteness like a held breath,
like the moment before the Virgin turns the corner
and is gone, and you are still reaching,
still twelve feet in the air on your father's shoulders,
believing the sorrow passing beneath you
is somehow also a form of light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective, sensory-rich monologue about love, spring, and the intoxicating smell of flowers filling a dark room.
counterfactuals.output:
The window was open before I noticed I had opened it—some part of me reaching toward the dark, toward the smell of things growing that had grown even without my permission, without my witnessing. Spring arrives like that, doesn't it, uninvited and total. I lay there in the dark room and let it in.

Hyacinth, I think. Or something close to it—something purple-throated and unbearably sweet, the kind of scent that has a texture, that seems to press against the skin rather than simply enter the nose. It filled the room the way water fills a cupped hand, finding every corner, every low place where the day's thoughts had settled and gone stale. I lay still and let myself be flooded.

This is what no one tells you about love: that it smells like something. That it has a season it prefers, a temperature at which it opens fully. I have loved in winter, dutifully, with my coat still on. But this—this dark room, this window, this green rush of scent moving over the sill like a tide coming in without any moon to command it—this is a different loving. The kind that undresses you slowly, that doesn't ask.

I think of hands. Not any particular hands, or perhaps all the hands I have ever wanted, folded now into this one imagined pressure against my collarbone, this weight that isn't there but might as well be, given how the flowers insist on it, given how the dark insists on it, given how spring never asks whether you are ready before it arrives with its whole green mouth open.

There is a kind of grief inside all this sweetness, I notice—the grief of things that must be blooming somewhere I cannot see, blooming without me, the way love always continues on past the borders of any one body holding it. The scent doesn't care whose window it enters. It doesn't care that I am alone here, gathering it into my chest like something I might keep.

But I don't try to keep it. I let it move through, the way you let a name move through you when you haven't said it in years and suddenly must. Petals I cannot see are doing something to the air, some alchemy of opening, and I am only the room they happen to be filling. The dark makes everything larger—unseen, the flowers could be endless, could be a whole field pressed up against the glass, could be spring itself deciding, tonight, to concentrate all its intention into this one small space where I happen to be lying, wanting, awake.

This is what I mean by love: not the hand, not the name, but this willingness to be entered by something sweet and unaccountable in the dark, to let a season do what seasons do, which is to insist that everything, even grief, even loneliness, even the ache of wanting hands that aren't there—

Even this can bloom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic reflection using vivid imagery of flowers, candlelight, and longing, ending with a metaphor about transparency and lightness.
counterfactuals.output:
# Waiting Room

The lilies open slow tonight,
white throats tilted toward the window
where no moon comes.

Candlelight pools like spilled honey
across the table's dark wood grain,
each flame a small orange tongue
speaking a language I've forgotten
how to answer.

I have been waiting so long
that waiting has become
its own kind of flower—
something with roots but no name,
petals that fold inward
when touched by expectation.

The wax weeps down in slow rivers.
Somewhere, a door I cannot see
almost opens.

Outside, the garden holds its breath.
Every bloom is a mouth
shaped around a word
that never quite arrives.

I think of you the way flame thinks of air—
necessary, unspoken,
a hunger with no hands.

And still the candles burn
toward morning,
toward whatever comes after longing
finally forgets what it was waiting for.

By then, perhaps,
I'll be like glass held up to light—
not empty, but so full of seeing through
that nothing casts a shadow anymore,
and even grief becomes
a kind of clarity,
weightless as the flame
that made it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness poem mixing nostalgia, nature imagery (skunk cabbage, lilies), and the emotional weight of love and spring.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thaw**

remember how the skunk cabbage broke through
before anything else dared, purple-hooded
ugly and brave in the retreating snow, how you
said even the ugly things want to live first—

spring again and I am unstitched by it, the way
mud smells like something confessing, the way
the creek behind your mother's house still runs
the same crooked mouth of water saying nothing
saying everything, saying *come back come back*

I keep finding you in the small violences of green—
the way tulip leaves knife up through dead leaves,
the way I used to trace your spine and call it
a riverbed, called your hands lily hands, white
and trembling and about to open

lilies later, always later, when the ground
has forgiven the frost, when the light stays long enough
to lie in, and you laughing somewhere in the doorframe
of memory, sun-warm, unaware you were already
becoming a season I'd have to survive—

funny how love works like skunk cabbage,
generates its own heat to melt the snow around it,
insists on blooming even where it stinks,
even where no one wanted it first,
even now, even after, even still

I am twenty springs deep in this ache
and the lilies keep opening their throats
like small elegies, like little easter mouths,
singing what I can't: that everything tender
comes back, that the ground remembers
what we buried in it, that you are
the season beneath all my seasons,
the green ache under the melting,
the first ugly flower of the year
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
